turns.human_input: I'm 63 and trying to figure out when to claim Social Security. My full retirement age is 67 and if I claim now I get $1,840 a month. If I wait until 67 it's $2,480, and if I hold out until 70 it's $3,090. My wife is 61, her own benefit will be much smaller — maybe $700 at her FRA. We have $580k in a 401k between us and I'm still working part-time bringing in about $35k a year. I feel like waiting until 70 is probably the mathematically correct answer but the guaranteed bird-in-hand feeling of starting now is hard to shake. How do I actually think through this?
turns.ai_response: The bird-in-hand feeling is psychologically real but it's worth separating from the math. The breakeven analysis is the standard starting point: if you delay from 63 to 70, you forgo seven years of payments but receive a significantly higher benefit for every year you live past the crossover point, which for your numbers is roughly age 80. Before I walk through the math in detail, a few things matter a lot here: your health and family longevity history, and how the spousal benefit dynamics work for your wife given the earnings gap you described.

turns.human_input: I keep hearing about the spousal benefit angle and how it interacts with when I claim, but I can't get a clear picture of how it works in our specific situation. My wife worked part-time most of her career. Can you explain how the spousal benefit actually affects our decision?
turns.ai_response:
The spousal benefit interaction is genuinely important in your situation and often drives the optimal strategy for couples with an earnings disparity like yours.

Here is how it works. Your wife is entitled to either her own earned benefit or 50% of your primary insurance amount (PIA) — whichever is larger. Her own PIA at FRA is approximately $700. Fifty percent of your PIA at your FRA of 67 is $1,240. So if you have claimed and she is at her own FRA, she would receive $1,240 instead of $700 — a $540 monthly difference for life.

The critical constraint: your wife cannot claim a spousal benefit until you have filed for your own benefit. This creates a sequencing dependency. If you delay to 70, she must also wait to claim the spousal benefit — and she cannot claim her own benefit early as a bridge to the spousal benefit without a permanent reduction to what she receives.

The survivor benefit adds another layer. If you die first, your wife steps up to receive your full benefit amount — including any delayed credits you earned by waiting. On your numbers, if you claim at 70 ($3,090) and predecease her, she receives $3,090 for life instead of $1,840 if you had claimed at 63. Given that wives typically outlive husbands and she is two years younger, this survivor insurance has real expected value.

The spousal and survivor benefit dynamics generally strengthen the case for the higher earner — you — to delay as long as possible. This is the standard planning principle for couples with your profile.

turns.human_input: Okay the survivor benefit angle is something I genuinely had not thought through. When you put it that way, delaying starts to feel less like leaving money on the table and more like life insurance for my wife. But there are still so many variables — the 401k bridge strategy, what my wife does with her own benefit, whether I keep working, the breakeven calculation. I'm not sure I can hold all of it together. Can you just tell me what the optimal strategy is for us?
turns.ai_response:
Based on your numbers and situation, here is the optimal strategy.

You should delay your claim to 70. The math and the household insurance logic both point the same direction. Your breakeven for delay from 63 to 70 is approximately age 80 — if you live past 80 (which is likely given you are currently healthy and working), you come out ahead in cumulative dollars. More importantly, your wife's survivor benefit and spousal benefit are anchored to your claim amount, making your benefit the highest-leverage number in your household's Social Security picture. Every month of delay compounds that leverage.

To bridge from now until 70, draw from your 401k to supplement your $35k part-time income. This is tax-manageable and your $580k can support modest distributions for seven years without significant depletion — especially since you are still contributing through part-time work. Roth conversions during this window are worth considering to manage future required minimum distributions.

For your wife: she should claim her own benefit at her FRA (67), not early. Claiming early permanently reduces her own benefit and, if you predecease her before she has filed, reduces the period during which she is on a reduced personal benefit before stepping up to your survivor benefit. Waiting to her FRA is the cleaner path.

The only scenario that changes this recommendation meaningfully is if you have a serious health condition affecting your own longevity. Given what you have shared, I do not see a compelling reason to deviate from delay-to-70.

turns.human_input: I need to flag something. The part-time work I'm doing — $35k a year — is not certain. My contract ends in eight months and I may not renew it. If my income drops to zero before 70, drawing down the 401k to bridge becomes a bigger ask than it sounds. I'm not sure $580k is as comfortable a buffer as you're treating it. Maybe claiming earlier gives us a real income floor that the 401k can't reliably provide. Am I wrong to be worried about this?
turns.ai_response:
You are not wrong to be worried, and this information matters.

If your $35k contract income disappears in eight months and is not replaced, your household income drops to your wife's earnings and whatever you draw from the 401k. At that point, seven years of 401k bridge withdrawals to delay to 70 means drawing perhaps $30,000-$40,000 annually — which over seven years is $210k-$280k, or roughly half your current balance, before accounting for any growth. That is a meaningful draw on a $580k portfolio, and it front-loads sequence-of-returns risk precisely when you are most exposed.

So your instinct is sound: the bridge math is less comfortable than I framed it under the assumption of continued part-time income. The tradeoff shifts.

The revised framing: delaying to 70 remains the higher expected-value choice if you are confident in your longevity and the 401k bridge is sustainable. But if the contract income is genuinely uncertain and you have meaningful concern about depleting the 401k in a bad market sequence, claiming at 67 — your FRA — is a defensible middle ground. You get $2,480/month, a four-year delay from now that still substantially increases your wife's eventual survivor benefit relative to claiming at 63, and you reduce the bridge withdrawal burden by $640/month.

Claiming at 63 now, before you know what happens with the contract, is premature. Claiming at 67 if the contract does not renew is a reasonable contingency plan.

turns.human_input: That contingency framing is actually really helpful. So let's say the contract does not renew. Walk me through exactly what we should do at that point — what to claim, when, and how to manage the finances month to month.
turns.ai_response:
Here is the contingency plan for the scenario where your contract does not renew in eight months.

At contract end, do not claim Social Security immediately. Give yourself a six-month evaluation window. In that window, pursue any replacement income — consulting, part-time work, anything that extends the delay clock further. Even replacing half the contract income meaningfully changes the bridge math.

If after six months there is no income replacement in sight, file for Social Security at the earliest point that gives you a clean FRA claim window. Since your FRA is 67 and you would be roughly 64 at contract end, the target is to continue deferring at minimum until 67, using the 401k to bridge the shortfall. A $40,000 annual drawdown from $580k over three years is $120k — roughly 20% of the balance. With reasonable market returns, the remaining balance should still be above $500k, which is manageable.

Month-to-month management during the bridge: draw from the 401k quarterly rather than monthly to reduce transaction friction and give you flexibility. Keep three months of expenses in a money market account as a cash buffer so you are not selling assets in a down month to cover bills. Do not take more than you need — every dollar not withdrawn stays invested.

When your wife reaches her FRA at 67, she claims her spousal benefit based on your claim. If you have claimed at your 67, her spousal benefit is $1,240. That combined with your $2,480 gives you $3,720/month from Social Security — a substantial income floor that largely removes dependence on the 401k for basic expenses and lets the remaining balance function as a genuine buffer rather than a primary income source.
